newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish shares discount uncertain steel price rise.
newsitem.headline: Swedish shares discount uncertain steel price rise.

text.p: The stock market's valuation of steel companies may be over optimistic with steel prices rising, but off historically low levels, industry analysts said on Thursday.
Steel companies have been expecting the stronger economy to push steel prices higher.
SSAB shares have risen 19 percent since July 24, Avesta Sheffield has jumped 23 percent and Sandvik's shares have gone up 12 percent.
Behind the rises is a belief that steel prices are to turn upwards during the autumn.
Merrill Lynch steel analyst Alan Coats agreed prices would rise, but said the levels would remain low.

"In my opinion the market is uninformed about the background to the development of steel prices. The large price fall from May 1995 to May 1996 continued, to nearly everyone's surprise, during the summer," he said.
"On the low levels that prices are at now there is a lot to indicate that the second half of 1996 could be worse, in terms of results, than the first half," Coats told Reuters.
Coats added that the strong Swedish crown did not help forecasts for the second half of 1996.
"The strengthening of the Swedish crown has come as an additional problem during a period when prices on rolled steel have fallen heavily.
"We could see an improvement in the market situation in October, but prices will still have a long way to go before reaching the level before the big fall," he said.
Another worrying factor was that the market upturn was not seen in other sectors which could work as a barometer for steel prices and steel companies' market opportunities.

"It is worrying that the truck market is still so weak. This does not sound good for a market where capital investments would need to show a boom in order for steel prices to return to acceptable levels."
Claes Vikbladh at Ohman brokerage was more optimistic, but even he said it was important to remember that the recovery would be from a low level.

"There are clear signs that price development has bottomed out. For one thing the market situation is the reverse compared to when prices began to fall with steel prices in the U.S., which lie 15-20 percent higher than European ones."
"Prices are still very low now and will probably not return to any record levels."
Vikbladh said the share market generally reacted faster to the first trend changes as no one wanted to slip behind if a turnaround were to occur.
"The future will tell if the share market has been right. On the positive side we have a continued growth in the U.S. economy and signs of a turnaround in Germany," said Vikbladh.
